speak.prosody: Chapter 5 The Power of Financial Education—Why Schools Don’t Teach Money Skills Isn’t it interesting? Schools spend years teaching us algebra, history, and science, but they almost never talk about money. Most people graduate knowing how to solve for X, but not how to manage a budget, invest in the stock market, or even start their own business. Because of this, a lot of young adults step into the real world feeling completely unprepared for the financial challenges ahead. This was something the boy noticed right away in his own life. His father was highly educated, with years of school and advanced degrees behind him, yet he often struggled with money. He knew how to earn a paycheck, but not how to make money work for him. On the other hand, the father of his friend—who had less formal schooling—seemed to have cracked the code when it came to building wealth. That contrast really made the boy think. Why do schools skip over financial education? It mostly comes down to tradition. Our education system was built for a different time, back when stable jobs and pensions were the norm. But things have changed. Job security isn’t what it used to be, and people who rely only on a steady paycheck can find themselves in trouble when layoffs or unexpected expenses hit. The friend’s father was convinced that understanding how money works is the most important skill you can learn. He encouraged the boys to read books, attend seminars, and find mentors who could teach them more. He always said that financial education isn’t something you do just once—it’s a lifelong journey. The world of money is always evolving, and if you stop learning, you’ll quickly fall behind. But he didn’t stop at just learning—he also talked about taking action. Knowledge by itself isn’t enough. It’s easy to read about investing or running a business, but you only really understand it when you try it for yourself. That might mean buying your first stock, starting a small business, or negotiating a deal. You’re bound to make mistakes along the way, but each mistake teaches you something you can’t learn from any textbook. Over time, the boy discovered that financial education is about more than just numbers. It’s also about your mindset, your habits, and your willingness to keep learning and growing. People who take charge of their own financial education start to see opportunities where everyone else sees obstacles. They become more resilient, more adaptable, and better equipped to build a life that’s not limited by fear or by the old rules.
